meta.title: Who really said "Change your life today. Don't gamble on the future, act now, without delay"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No. This rhyming motivational line traces to a modern quote compilation, not to Simone de Beauvoir. It appears in none of her books, essays, or interviews.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Change your life today. Don't gamble on the future, act now, without delay'?
meta.ogDescription: A feel-good rhyme pinned on Simone de Beauvoir. It's in none of her works — its only trail is a 2007 quotation compilation. Verdict: unsourced, not verified.

answer.label: Not verified as Simone de Beauvoir — an unsourced modern line
answer.authorDates: No source in Simone de Beauvoir’s works; earliest trail is a 2007 quotation compilation
answer.sourceLine: This rhyming couplet is pinned on Simone de Beauvoir all over the web, but it appears in none of her books, essays, diaries, or interviews. The only “source” anyone cites is Wikiquote’s Attributed section, which itself points only to John Cook’s motivational compilation The Book of Positive Quotations — not to de Beauvoir. The English internal rhyme (“today … delay”) is a further red flag, since her work was written in French and any genuine quote would be a translation.

source.excerpt: Change your life today. Don’t gamble on the future, act now, without delay.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line under Attributed — explicitly not its Sourced section — citing only The Book of Positive Quotations (2007) by John Cook, p. 548, a modern motivational anthology.
Goodreads likewise attributes it to The Book of Positive Quotations, a compilation — not to any book de Beauvoir wrote.
Aggregators such as buboquote and BrainyQuote reproduce the line with de Beauvoir’s name and no primary source at all — no title, page or date.
No Quote Investigator study attributes this wording to de Beauvoir, and it surfaces in none of her collected works — consistent with a modern, anonymously-authored motivational rhyme.
source.excerptNote: Presented everywhere as a standalone aphorism, with no surrounding passage, work, chapter or date — the typical signature of a quotation-site invention rather than an extract from a real text.

author.name: Simone de Beauvoir
author.heading: About Simone de Beauvoir
author.bio: Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was a French existentialist philosopher, novelist and feminist theorist, best known for The Second Sex (1949) and the memoir Memoirs of a Dutiful Daughter (1958). Her real writing is dense, analytical French prose about freedom, ambiguity and the situation of women — nothing like a rhyming self-help slogan. Because her name carries philosophical authority, it has become a magnet for feel-good lines she never wrote, of which this is one.

misattribution.heading: Why this gets pinned on de Beauvoir
misattribution.intro: A rhyming pep-talk with no citation, laundered through a quote book and then stamped with a famous philosopher’s name.

items.why: Presented as her words across quote sites, yet the phrase appears in none of her books, essays, diaries or interviews. Wikiquote keeps it in “Attributed,” not “Sourced.”

items.who: The Book of Positive Quotations (John Cook, comp.)
items.why: Every trail ends at this modern motivational anthology, which lists the line under de Beauvoir’s name without a primary reference — as Goodreads itself shows. A compilation attesting a quote is not evidence she said it.

misattribution.truthLine: There is no evidence Simone de Beauvoir ever wrote or said this. Its English internal rhyme and its trail ending at a modern quotation compilation mark it as an unsourced motivational line, not a genuine de Beauvoir sentence.

context.heading: A rhyme is the tell
lead: Simone de Beauvoir wrote in French, in long analytical sentences about freedom and the “situation” of women. A tidy English couplet that rhymes — today / delay — cannot survive translation from French unless someone rebuilt it as verse, which is exactly what motivational writers, not philosophers, do.

The likeliest story is mundane: an anonymous carpe-diem rhyme got printed in a quotation anthology beside de Beauvoir’s name, and the internet did the rest. Absent any dated work, chapter or page, the honest verdict is that this is not a verified de Beauvoir quote.
context.pull: A rhyming pep-talk in English is not how de Beauvoir wrote in French.
